title: Don't despair of mercy (Berakhot 10a)
hook: Hezekiah: even with a sword on your neck, don't give up on mercy
tomorrow: why would a king say the same line five times?

segments.voice: Yesterday, four cubits: with the Temple gone, God's place became person-sized. Today, a king in a small room, facing a wall.

The test results come back, and the doctor's face says it before the words do. Some people go quiet; some get very practical. Berakhot tells of a king who got that kind of news from a prophet, and the first thing he did was talk back.
screen: `THE NEWS BEFORE THE WORDS.` → `QUIET, OR PRACTICAL.` → `A KING TALKS BACK.`

segments.voice: Isaiah comes to King Hezekiah, who is sick, and says, in the Jewish Publication Society's words: "Set thy house in order; for thou shalt die, and not live." The Talmud imagines Hezekiah's reply: son of Amoz, finish your prophecy and go. I have a teaching from my ancestor's house: even if a sharp sword rests on a person's neck, he should not hold himself back from asking for mercy. Then, in the book of Isaiah, Hezekiah turns his face to the wall and prays, and God answers that the prayer was heard, and adds years to his life. One question for today: when is it too late to hope? The Talmud's answer: not while you can still ask. Here's the unity thread. The Qur'an says something close, in its own words. In Pickthall's translation, God tells those who have wronged themselves: "Despair not of the mercy of Allah." Two traditions, one refusal: mercy isn't closed while a person is still turning toward it. And the honest difference. Hezekiah, facing death, asks for more life; his story is about danger. The Qur'an's verse speaks to people weighed down by what they've done; it's about forgiveness. Same door, different rooms behind it. One to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, a king tells a prophet to finish talking, because he still has a prayer to say.
screen: `SET THY HOUSE IN ORDER.` · `A SWORD ON THE NECK: STILL ASK.` · `DESPAIR NOT OF THE MERCY OF ALLAH.` · `SAME DOOR, DIFFERENT ROOMS.` · then, large: `DON'T DESPAIR OF MERCY.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and write, by hand, one hard thing you're facing, in a single line. Underneath it, write one small thing you can still ask for inside it: help, time, a better day. Rest your eyes on that second line for the whole sit.
screen: `ONE HARD THING.` · `ONE THING YOU CAN STILL ASK.`

segments.voice: Don't despair of mercy. Hezekiah's teaching: even with a sword on your neck, keep asking.
For the hard days: don't despair of mercy, not while you can still ask. Berakhot, day ten.

fork.setup: a friend got turned down by every school she applied to and says there's no point asking for anything now. what does Hezekiah's line point to?
options: keep asking: an appeal, a waitlist, another door. it's not over while she can ask.
accept it quietly; a decision like that is final, like a prophet's word.
stop hoping for a while; asking again will only hurt her more.
fork.reveal: Hezekiah heard 'you will die' from a prophet and still turned to the wall to pray. the Talmud's line: even with a sword on your neck, don't hold back from asking.

what it means: even at the edge, don't stop asking for mercy; hope isn't a promise, it's the refusal to stop asking.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 10a gives Hezekiah a teaching 'from my ancestor's house', often read as David's; Isaiah 38 and 2 Kings 20 tell the illness and the answered prayer.
guess: even at the very edge, keep asking for mercy
mercy goes only to those who never lose hope
never let other people see that you're afraid

chat.meaning: Hezekiah won't stop asking, even with a sword on his neck. Hope here isn't a promise of how it ends; it's not giving up on mercy.
